content: 1. Observational studies that rely on registered diagnoses may have excluded a significant number of eligible participants who exhibit nonspecific or unclear adverse symptoms. This is particularly relevant as many young girls reporting adverse events following HPV vaccination often do not receive a clinical diagnosis and, therefore, are unlikely to be included in medical registries. 2. Randomized clinical trials evaluating the safety of HPV vaccines have been criticized for not using true placebos, such as those without adjuvants, as the control intervention. 3. Adjuvants are substances added to vaccines to enhance the immune response to weak antigens and improve the overall efficacy of the vaccine. 4. Adjuvants can also provide additional benefits, such as reducing the frequency of vaccinations, lowering the antigen dose per vaccine, offering cross-clade immunity (protection against different virus or bacterial clades), and improving the stability of the final vaccine formulation. 5. Currently, five adjuvants with distinct mechanisms of action are approved for vaccine production: aluminum salts (EU, US), MF59 (EU), AS03 (EU), AS04 (EU, US), and virosomes (EU). 6. Virosomes are composed of a lipid membrane incorporating virus-derived proteins, while MF59 and AS03 are squalene-based adjuvants. AS04 combines aluminum hydroxide with monophosphoryl lipid A. 7. Aluminum salts, commonly referred to as alum, are the most widely used adjuvants and include aluminum potassium sulfate, aluminum hydroxide, aluminum phosphate, and amorphous aluminum hydroxyphosphate sulfate. 8. Insoluble aluminum salts have been used as vaccine adjuvants since 1926, with aluminum potassium sulfate being the first. However, due to poor reproducibility, it has been largely replaced by aluminum hydroxide and aluminum phosphate, which are more standardized and capable of directly adsorbing antigens. 9. Aluminum has been the standard adjuvant in vaccines for diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal conjugates, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B. 10. More recently, aluminum has been co-formulated with HPV vaccines in the form of AS04, which contains aluminum hydroxide and amorphous aluminum hydroxyphosphate sulfate. 11. Amorphous aluminum hydroxyphosphate sulfate is commercially produced at the nanometer scale and represents one of the latest marketed aluminum adjuvants. 12. The mechanism of action of aluminum as an adjuvant is poorly understood, and prevailing theories evolve with new insights into immunology and the physicochemical properties of aluminum. 13. Despite incomplete understanding, the repeated use of aluminum in vaccines is justified by its apparent safety profile, ease of preparation, stability, potent immunostimulatory ability, and the lack of suitable alternatives. 14. Aluminum is the third most abundant element in the Earth's crust but has no known biological or physiological role. It is absorbed into the bloodstream through the gastrointestinal tract and is rapidly eliminated by the kidneys and bile. 15. While aluminum is considered safe and regularly ingested through food and water, it is toxic at high concentrations. Its toxicity depends not only on concentration but also on its chemical form and environmental factors. 16. In the bloodstream, aluminum binds to transferrin with high affinity, competing with iron at the binding site. It also affects cellular processes and physiological functions, such as competing with magnesium for membrane transporters, disrupting calcium metabolism, increasing oxidative stress, and binding to nucleoside phosphate groups, amino acids, and membrane lipids. 17. At high concentrations, aluminum predominantly accumulates in bone and brain tissue. Animal and human studies have shown it to act as a potent neurological toxicant and to provoke toxic effects in fetuses and embryos when exposure occurs during pregnancy. 18. Recent data suggest that aluminum can cross the blood-brain barrier by directly affecting cerebral blood vessels. 19. Despite its unclear biological role, aluminum appears to impact the immune system, making it useful as a vaccine adjuvant. It binds antigens with high affinity and was initially thought to function by forming a depot at the injection site, allowing for a high antigen concentration and continuous antigen release. 20. Aluminum is now believed to exert its adjuvant effects by stimulating Th2-type immune responses, promoting antibody production through B cell activation, activating the complement system, and recruiting immune cells to the injection site. 21. At the injection site, aluminum facilitates antigen uptake by specialized antigen-presenting immune cells called dendritic cells and promotes their maturation. 22. The size of adjuvant particles significantly influences the immune response. Aluminum hydroxide adjuvant particles are approximately 100 nm in size, while aluminum phosphate particles are around 50 nm. In aqueous solutions, these particles aggregate to form microscale-sized particulates ranging from 1 to 20 µm. 23. Aluminum hydroxide and aluminum phosphate can be produced at nanoscale sizes (≤200 nm), but currently, only amorphous aluminum hydroxyphosphate sulfate is produced at the nanoscale for vaccine preparations. 24. Particle size is directly linked to the efficiency of antigen adsorption. Nanoscale aluminum particles can adsorb more antigens than traditional aluminum-based adjuvants due to their higher surface-area-to-volume ratio and are more potent than traditional microparticles. 25. The efficiency of particle uptake by dendritic cells in vitro and in vivo is inversely proportional to particle size, with maximum efficiency observed for nanoscale particles smaller than 100 nm. 26. Dendritic cells are specialized immune cells that scavenge and engulf particles smaller than 10 µm, having evolved to recognize pathogens of this size. 27. Other factors, such as particle structure, shape, and surface charge, also significantly influence uptake by dendritic cells.
